div.head: ECf 32 E
div.ab: De iure et de appendiciis corone regni Britannie. Arturus uero, qui fuit quondam inclitissimus rex Britonum, uir magnus fuit et animosus et miles illustris. Parum fuit ei regnum istud; non fuit contentus animus eius regno Britannie excessitque metas et fines regni huius, et subiugauit sibi uiriliter et strenue Scanciam totam, que modo Norweya uocatur, et omnes insulas ultra Scanciam, scilicet Islandiam et Grenelandiam, que sunt de appendiciis Norweye, et Suetheidam et Hiberniam et Gutlandiam et Daciam et Semelandiam et Wynelandiam et Curlandiam et Roe et Fenielandiam et Wirlandiam et Estlandiam et Cherrelam et Lappam et omnes alias terras et insulas orientales occeani usque Russiam — in Lappam scilicet posuit orientalem metam regni Britannie — et multas alias insulas ultra Scanciam, usquedum sub septemtrione, que sunt de appendiciis Scanciae, que modo Norweia uocatur.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 659 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints across the page as an insertion into ECf retr. 32 (32 A–E, pp. 655–660). The dictionary cites it as “ECf 32 …”, so it is kept with ECf here.

Schwerlich redet er nur aus Nationalstolz oder um gelehrt zu prunken; vielmehr möchte er wohl Englands Activhandel in Nordischen und Baltischen Ländern historisch begründen; Londons Handel mit Russland und Norwegen bezeugt Wil. fil. Greenland; the Londoner probably heard the following names from North Germans or Scandinavians. He hardly speaks merely out of national pride or to show off his learning; rather he probably wants to give a historical foundation to England’s active trade in the Norse and Baltic lands; London’s trade with Russia and Norway is attested by Wil. fil. div.ab: Concerning the right and the appurtenances of the crown of the kingdom of Britain. Arthur, who was once the most renowned king of the Britons, was a great man and courageous and an illustrious knight. This kingdom was too little for him; his spirit was not content with the kingdom of Britain, and he went beyond the bounds and borders of this kingdom, and manfully and vigorously subjugated to himself the whole of Scancia, which is now called Norway, and all the islands beyond Scancia, namely Iceland and Greenland, which are among the appurtenances of Norway, and Sweden and Ireland and Gotland and Denmark and Semeland and Wineland and Courland and Roe and Finland and Wirland and Estland and Cherrela and Lapland and all the other eastern lands and islands of the ocean as far as Russia — in Lapland, namely, he placed the eastern boundary of the kingdom of Britain — and many other islands beyond Scancia, as far as under the north, which are among the appurtenances of Scancia, which is now called Norway.
